assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built the modern field of political economics, integrating electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal policy into a coherent theoretical and empirical research program. It has shaped macro, public and development economics, and the evidence base is broad.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are central through their theory and comparative-constitutions work. Besley is central through state capacity and the empirical political-economy agenda. Others (e.g. Acemoglu, Robinson, Alesina) are outside the credited names, so the three-person cap is a clean but imperfect cut.
assessment.maturity: Decades of cumulative work, the field is well established, and the results have been replicated and extended. The timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer to frame the contribution through a different set of individuals.
Some constitutional-effects findings rest on observational identification.
Committee-affiliation conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices, plus dynamic oligopoly estimation, turned empirical IO into a practical tool used in merger review, antitrust, trade and health. The methodological and policy influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: The BLP framework (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is the clearest core. Bresnahan, Reiss, Levin, Benkard and others made important parallel or related contributions, so a three-person limit omits meaningful credit.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1990s and has been confirmed by three decades of widespread use. It is fully mature.
uncertainties: Credit is divided between demand estimation and dynamic-games work.
Bresnahan's contribution could reasonably displace one of the proposed names.
The field-specific appeal to a committee that includes IO expertise should not be taken as merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Developed the New Keynesian framework and the modern theory of monetary policy, covering nominal rigidities, policy rules and the microfounded welfare analysis that central banks now use. The influence on practice is very strong.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many contributors, including Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Galí, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum. Any three-person selection is contestable, and Gertler's earlier recognition (2022) complicates his inclusion.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of practical use in monetary policy and many empirical tests, although the post-2021 inflation episode has prompted debate.
uncertainties: Attribution among many plausible contributors is hard.
Calvo or Christiano and Eichenbaum could be preferred over those selected.
The framework's performance during the recent inflation has been debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combined the task-based view of technology with credible evidence on how trade shocks and automation reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets. The work has changed both academic and policy understanding of inequality and globalization.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central in both the task approach and the China-shock work. Hanson and Dorn are central to the China-shock identification. Katz's contributions to the skill-premium literature are also substantial, and the task-model theory involves others outside the list (Acemoglu, Restrepo).
assessment.maturity: The work has been influential for 10–20 years. The China-shock findings have been replicated and refined, though the effects of automation and the long-run persistence of trade effects are still debated.
uncertainties: Credit for the task framework partly lies outside the credited names.
Whether the China-shock magnitudes are robust across specifications and countries.
The Katz-or-Dorn trade-off within the three-name limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The firm-heterogeneity framework changed trade theory and measurement by explaining exporter selection, reallocation and a new source of gains from trade. It underlies a very large empirical literature and informs trade-policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the central contribution, and Helpman brought heterogeneous firms into the new trade theory. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, among others, contributed important empirical and theoretical parallels outside the credited names. Redding's contribution is substantive but later.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of work that has been widely extended and tested. Very mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with other trade candidates (B003, B041) and uncertainty about how the Committee would divide credit.
Credit for the empirical foundations (Bernard, Jensen and others) lies outside the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reconstructed long-run series on top incomes and wealth and offshore wealth using tax data. This changed the empirical basis and public debate on distribution and also influenced measurement practice (e.g. distributional national accounts). Its influence on the field is great, though the conceptual and theoretical novelty is thinner than the data contribution.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the pioneers of the top-incomes series, and Zucman extended this to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson, who is deceased, was a precursor and co-founder of the field, and the World Inequality Database involves many collaborators.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work is over twenty years old and has been widely used. Some wealth-concentration and offshore estimates, and their interpretation, are still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of wealth-distribution estimates and of the capital-return interpretation.
Atkinson's deceased status and the omission of other contributors.
Saez also appears under B007, which affects portfolio overlap.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantitative Ricardian models turned trade theory into a tool for measuring welfare gains and counterfactuals, via sufficient-statistics results and Eaton-Kortum structure. They are widely used in policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Kortum is the key figure through Eaton-Kortum, but Jonathan Eaton is not among the credited names, which is a significant gap. Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare are central to the later quantification and gains-from-trade work, along with Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The approach is well established, with about two decades of applications, though parts of the newer work are still being tested.
uncertainties: Missing Eaton, and the question of whether the credited set reflects a sound division of credit.
Reliance on strong structural assumptions for the welfare measurements.
Overlap with other trade candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification provides a principled way to draw credible inferences under weak assumptions, and it clarified the trade-off between assumptions and conclusions. It has had a strong effect on econometric methodology, on applied work with incomplete data and on the interpretation of policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the founder and by far the leading figure. Tamer and Molinari are central to the later inference and moment-inequality theory, with Chernozhukov, Hong, Tamer and others outside the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Manski's work is over thirty years old and the framework is firmly part of the econometric canon, though practical adoption in applied work is uneven.
uncertainties: A single-laureate award for Manski may be more apt than a three-person one.
Uneven uptake in applied economics.
Competition from other econometrics candidates with greater empirical impact.
